title: Gram-Positive Cocci: Staph and Strep Essentials

cards.front: Which test separates staphylococci from streptococci, and what are the expected results?
cards.back: Catalase test. Staphylococci/micrococci = positive (bubbles); streptococci/enterococci = negative.

cards.front: What does a positive tube coagulase test indicate, and when is it read?
cards.back: Free coagulase production by Staphylococcus aureus; a fibrin clot at 4 hours or 18-24 hours is positive.

cards.front: Slide coagulase detects [[1]]; tube coagulase detects [[2]]. A negative slide test must be confirmed by [[3]].
cards.back: 1: bound clumping factor  2: free coagulase  3: tube coagulase or validated latex method

cards.front: How is Streptococcus pyogenes (group A) identified on the bench?
cards.back: Beta-hemolytic, catalase negative, bacitracin susceptible, PYR positive.

cards.front: Which three tests identify Streptococcus agalactiae (group B)?
cards.back: Beta-hemolysis, CAMP positive (arrowhead hemolysis), hippurate hydrolysis positive (bacitracin resistant).

cards.front: Streptococcus pneumoniae is alpha-hemolytic, [[1]] susceptible, and [[2]] soluble.
cards.back: 1: optochin  2: bile

cards.front: Which two reactions confirm Enterococcus species?
cards.back: Bile esculin hydrolysis positive (blackening) and growth in 6.5 percent NaCl.

cards.front: How do viridans streptococci differ from pneumococci on bench tests?
cards.back: Viridans: optochin resistant, bile esculin negative. Pneumococcus: optochin susceptible, bile soluble.

cards.front: PYR positive organisms are [[1]] and [[2]].
cards.back: 1: Streptococcus pyogenes  2: Enterococcus species

cards.front: Which coagulase-negative staphylococcus is novobiocin resistant and a urinary pathogen of young women?
cards.back: Staphylococcus saprophyticus (note: routine novobiocin testing is largely replaced by rapid ID systems; follow local procedure).

cards.front: Why can picking colonies from sheep blood agar give a false-positive catalase?
cards.back: Erythrocytes contain catalase; a red-cell-rich inoculum can bubble with hydrogen peroxide.

cards.front: S. aureus colonies are often [[1]] pigmented and [[2]]-hemolytic; coagulase-negative staphylococci are usually coagulase [[3]].
cards.back: 1: golden  2: beta  3: negative

cards.front: What does the CAMP test detect and what does a positive look like?
cards.back: Synergy between group B streptococcus CAMP factor and staphylococcal beta-lysin; an arrowhead zone of enhanced hemolysis.

cards.front: What is the classic Gram stain morphology of Streptococcus pneumoniae?
cards.back: Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci (often in pairs, sometimes short chains).

cards.front: Beta-hemolytic + bacitracin [[1]] + PYR [[2]] = Streptococcus pyogenes.
cards.back: 1: susceptible  2: positive

cards.front: Why is identifying group B streptococcus in a pregnant patient clinically important?
cards.back: It guides intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent neonatal sepsis and meningitis.

cards.front: A mixed wound culture grows staphylococci and streptococci. How should it be reported?
cards.back: Report both identifications with a comment about mixed flora and correlate with Gram stain and clinical findings (per local procedure).

cards.front: Bile esculin positive + 6.5 percent NaCl growth = [[1]]. Optochin susceptible + bile soluble = [[2]].
cards.back: 1: Enterococcus  2: Streptococcus pneumoniae

title: Gram-Negative Rods, Sterile Sites, and AST Essentials

cards.front: What is the first biochemical split for gram-negative rods and what does each result mean?
cards.back: Oxidase test. Oxidase negative + glucose fermenter = Enterobacterales; oxidase positive = Pseudomonas/Aeromonas/Vibrio-type organisms.

cards.front: What biochemical profile identifies Escherichia coli in a lactose-fermenting oxidase-negative rod?
cards.back: Indole positive, citrate negative, urease negative (lysine usually positive).

cards.front: Triple sugar iron: the butt reflects [[1]] fermentation; the slant reflects [[2]] and [[3]] fermentation. Blackening indicates [[4]].
cards.back: 1: glucose  2: lactose  3: sucrose  4: hydrogen sulfide (H2S)

cards.front: Which reactions identify Klebsiella pneumoniae?
cards.back: Mucoid lactose fermenter, indole negative, citrate positive, VP positive, urease positive (slow).

cards.front: What are the classic bench clues for Proteus species?
cards.back: Strong rapid urease, swarming motility, phenylalanine deaminase positive; P. mirabilis indole negative, P. vulgaris indole positive.

cards.front: Salmonella on TSI shows [[1]] slant and [[2]] butt with [[3]] blackening; it is lysine [[4]].
cards.back: 1: alkaline (red)  2: acid (yellow)  3: H2S  4: positive

cards.front: How does Shigella differ from Salmonella on key tests?
cards.back: Shigella is non-motile, H2S negative (no TSI blackening), and lysine negative; Salmonella is usually motile, H2S positive, lysine positive.

cards.front: What are the calling-card features of Pseudomonas aeruginosa?
cards.back: Oxidase positive, grape-like odor, green pyocyanin pigment, growth at 42 degrees Celsius, non-lactose fermenter.

cards.front: Acinetobacter baumannii complex appears as gram-negative [[1]] in pairs, is oxidase [[2]], and is [[3]] (non-motile).
cards.back: 1: coccobacilli  2: negative  3: non-motile

cards.front: What CSF pattern suggests bacterial meningitis?
cards.back: Neutrophilic pleocytosis, low CSF glucose (below about 40 mg/dL or below about 60 percent of paired serum), high protein; intervals vary by laboratory and age.

cards.front: What is the recommended blood culture collection practice?
cards.back: At least two sets from separate venipunctures, ideally before antibiotics; blood culture bottles are drawn first in the order of draw.

cards.front: MIC is the lowest antimicrobial concentration that prevents [[1]]; the lowest concentration that kills is the [[2]].
cards.back: 1: visible growth  2: minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC)

cards.front: How are disk diffusion zone diameters interpreted?
cards.back: Against current clinical breakpoints from CLSI or EUCAST (state which standard and version); verify with QC strains such as E. coli ATCC 25922.

cards.front: How is MRSA confirmed in the laboratory?
cards.back: Cefoxitin disk susceptibility (surrogate for mecA) plus PBP2a latex agglutination or mecA molecular detection.

cards.front: Under current EUCAST wording, category I means [[1]], and laboratories must state whether [[2]] or [[3]] breakpoints are used.
cards.back: 1: susceptible, increased exposure  2: EUCAST  3: CLSI

cards.front: What specimen handling is essential for anaerobic culture?
cards.back: Oxygen-free transport systems, prompt inoculation onto pre-reduced media, incubation under anaerobic conditions.

cards.front: Which stain screens concentrated sputum for mycobacteria with the best sensitivity?
cards.back: Auramine O fluorescent stain (confirmed with Ziehl-Neelsen); culture remains the gold standard.

cards.front: Clavulanate synergy with cephalosporins confirms [[1]]. Cefoxitin disk plus PBP2a confirms [[2]].
cards.back: 1: extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)  2: methicillin resistance (MRSA)
